title: The Bridge That Needed Fewer Warning Signs
passage:
A pedestrian bridge over a railway line had a low beam near one entrance. Tall cyclists who rode across the bridge sometimes hit the beam if they did not lower their heads. Riding bicycles on the narrow bridge was already prohibited, and several warning signs told cyclists to get off and walk. Despite the signs, some continued riding. The city responded after each minor accident by adding another warning.

Within a few years, the entrance contained six different signs: ‘Walk Your Bicycle,’ ‘Low Clearance,’ ‘Slow Down,’ ‘Watch Your Head,’ a height measurement, and a picture of a bicycle with a red line through it. Officials assumed more warnings meant more safety. Residents complained that the entrance looked confusing and that none of the signs stood out.

A safety engineer reviewed the site. She agreed that cyclist behavior was part of the problem but questioned the sign strategy. People approaching the bridge had only a few seconds to notice, read, and act. Six competing messages required more attention than one clear instruction. She also noticed that the bridge entrance visually resembled the continuation of the bicycle path. Nothing in the physical design strongly suggested that riders should stop.

The city tested a redesign. Most signs were removed. A single large ground marking said ‘DISMOUNT’ with a bicycle symbol before the entrance. A short textured strip made the surface feel different under wheels, and a narrow railing created a slight turn that encouraged cyclists to slow down. One height warning remained beside the low beam.

Some residents worried that removing signs would reduce legal protection or make the danger less visible. The city checked the required safety standards and kept the mandatory notices, but eliminated duplicated messages that were not required. Accident reports and video observations were collected for six months.

The number of cyclists entering at full speed decreased. Not everyone dismounted, but more slowed before reaching the beam. Near-miss incidents also fell. Researchers could not say which part of the redesign produced most of the change because the signs, pavement, and railing were altered together. The city accepted this limitation because the practical goal was safer behavior, not proving the effect of one element.

The project challenged the assumption that adding information always increases safety. A warning competes for limited attention. When many warnings overlap, each may become less noticeable. Physical design can also communicate expected behavior before words are read. The new entrance made slowing down feel natural rather than relying entirely on obedience to signs.

The engineer emphasized that fewer signs should not become a universal rule. Some hazards genuinely require several kinds of information. The lesson was more careful: every warning should have a clear purpose, and repeated warnings should not substitute for fixing confusing design. Safety communication is strongest when the environment, the instruction, and the action people need to take all point in the same direction.
translation:
線路をまたぐ歩道橋の入口近くには低い梁があり、自転車に乗ったまま通る背の高い人が頭をぶつけることがありました。橋は狭く自転車走行は禁止されており、『降りて押してください』などの看板もありましたが、事故のたびに市はさらに警告看板を追加していました。

数年後、入口には『自転車を押す』『頭上注意』『減速』『低い梁』『高さ表示』『自転車禁止マーク』など六種類が並びました。情報を増やせば安全になると考えられていましたが、住民からは多すぎて何も目立たないという声が出ました。

安全技術者が見ると、接近する数秒の間に六つの内容を読み行動するのは難しく、さらに自転車道がそのまま橋へ続いて見えるため、物理的にも『ここで止まる』という印象が弱いことが分かりました。

そこで大部分の重複看板を外し、入口手前の路面に大きく『降りる』と自転車マークを表示しました。車輪で分かる質感の違う帯を置き、短い柵でわずかに進路を曲げ、自然に減速するようにしました。低い梁の高さ警告は残しました。

看板を減らすと法的に問題ではないかという心配もありましたが、必要な表示は残し、義務でない重複だけを外しました。六か月の観察では高速のまま入る自転車が減り、降りない人でも減速する割合が増え、接触寸前の例も減りました。複数要素を同時に変えたため、どれが最も効いたかは断定できませんが、実際の安全改善が目的なので市はその限界を受け入れました。

この事例は、情報を増やせば安全が高まるとは限らないことを示します。警告は限られた注意力を奪い合い、多すぎると一つ一つが弱くなります。また、言葉を読む前に物理的環境そのものが行動を伝えることもできます。

ただし『看板は少ないほどよい』という一般則ではありません。複数情報が必要な危険もあります。大切なのは、各警告に明確な役割があり、重複看板で分かりにくい設計を隠さないことです。環境、指示、必要行動が同じ方向を示すとき、安全な伝達は最も強くなります。
